about: Questions an engineer or operator asks of a plant drawing, as data. scripts/question_engine.py runs them over a process model or an extracted twin and writes, for each item a question applies to, the evidence found, the data still needed and where to get it, how the data settles the question, and what a public source says the typical benefit is. A screen, not an audit: it computes no savings for any plant. Rules E1-E26 and C1-C10 follow a research review of public DOE, LBNL, EPA and HSE sources (wording copied from text extracts of those documents); H1-H4 (high-grade heat used for low-grade duty) were added on request and cite the closest source wording, saying so where no number exists. E27-E32, H5, H6, C11 and C12 (refrigeration, ovens, dryers and fryers) were added from a food manufacturer's walkthrough; each quotes S25-S28 with a page, checked word for word against the PDF named in the source's 'checked' note. IAC/ITAC statistics are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch, not re-verified against the download; average dollar figures are deliberately left out. See docs/OPPORTUNITY_SCREEN.md.

families.heat_grade: Heat grade (high-grade heat for low-grade duty)

fields_help.applies_when: absent_note: a sentence quoted as evidence saying what was looked for and not found. anchor: a selector (or list of selectors, any may match) for the item that triggers the question. with: clauses that must all find a related item. without: clauses of which none may find one. also_show: related items quoted as evidence if present. group_by: unit | item | model. needs_model: item kinds the model must contain, else the question is reported as not checked. min_anchors: fewest triggering items per group.
fields_help.selector: kind (equipment, instrument, valve = control valve, final_element = other operated valve or speed element, hand_valve, relief, controller, interlock, stream, line_item, offpage), type (exact), type_text (regex over type and text), isa (regex over ISA letters), variable, text (regex over tag, name, description and schedule service), text_all (all regexes), not_text, tagged, control_valve, fact_C_min / fact_C_max (a stated temperature fact), schedule_field (the drawing prints this field, filled or blank).
fields_help.relation: same_unit, same_stream, same_unit_same_medium (same unit and same utility: steam, cooling water, air...), other_unit, discharge_side (streams leaving the anchor's unit; on an extracted twin, within max_hops drawn links on the same sheet, direction unknown), near (same unit or stream; on a twin within max_hops links), drives (a controller writing to the anchor), reads (a controller or interlock reading the anchor), anywhere, linked (on a hand-built model: a stream drawn from or to the anchor's unit, an item on such a stream, or the equipment at its other end; on an extracted twin, within max_hops drawn links like near). twin_only / hand_only: true limits a clause to extracted twins / hand-built models. anchor_kind: the clause applies only to anchors of these kinds.
fields_help.data_requests: item, fields (names looked up in the model's facts and the equipment schedule: present = quoted as evidence; printed but blank = the request names that field on that sheet's schedule; a request stays open while any of its fields is still missing), where (ordered, most direct first: historian (for a role; quantity = flow, temperature, pressure, power, composition or position names only signals that measure it, so a valve position is never offered as a flow; match = a regex the item must match), dcs, nameplate, vendor, maintenance, records, bills, walkdown, or free text), how.
fields_help.typical_benefit: wording copied from the source, source keys, arc = DOE IAC/ITAC recommendation code where mapped. Never a figure for a specific plant.

screen_exclusions.reason: nuclear reactor coolant, chemical and volume control and residual heat removal systems: safety-related design changes go through the licensing basis, not an energy or controls screen

questions.question: Is this pump throttled by a control valve when it could run on a variable speed drive?

applies_when.absent_note: no speed control (SC, SIC, SY tag, VFD or VSD) on or next to the pump

also_show.as: other control valve on the discharge

evidence_fields: control valve tag on the discharge

data_requests.item: Control valve position (% open) over normal operation

where.what: the valve's controller output
read the positioner stroke indicator at several rates

data_requests.how: Take a month or more of valve output at normal sampling; note the typical and the lowest % open, and the hours at each.

data_requests.item: Flow over the same period (a flow-duration curve)

where.what: production rate records

data_requests.how: Bin the flow into ranges and count the hours in each.

where.what: pump curve and rated duty point
pump

data_requests.how: Copy the rated flow and head and get the pump curve.

where.what: motor
motor record card

data_requests.how: Copy rated power, speed and efficiency from the motor nameplate.

where.what: elevations and pressures at the suction source and the delivery point
line list or isometrics for pipe lengths and sizes

data_requests.how: Static head = lift plus pressure difference between source and destination; the rest of the pump head at duty is friction plus the valve drop.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a drive quote when the valve normally runs well throttled for long hours and most of the head is friction rather than static lift (VSDs suit friction-dominated systems best). Close it if the valve normally runs near fully open, the head is mostly static, or the pump runs few hours.

typical_benefit.wording: "With rotodynamic pump installations, savings of between 30% and 50% have been achieved in many installations by installing VSDs." Also: "It is estimated that 75% of pump systems are oversized, many by more than 20%."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4146 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 5,227 recommendations, 3.0 yr average payback, 31.4% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: On a hand-built model the valve sits on a stream leaving the pump. On an extracted drawing the links have no direction, so the rule takes a control valve within four drawn links that do not pass through other equipment; it may still be on a branch or the suction side, so check the drawing. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is this pump oversized, given a bypass line around it or its valve?
evidence_fields: bypass line or valve near the pump

data_requests.item: Measured flow and head at normal operation

where.what: suction and discharge pressure gauges plus a clamp-on ultrasonic flow meter

data_requests.how: Read flow and suction and discharge pressure at steady operation.

where.what: pump curve

data_requests.how: Read BEP flow and head from the curve.

data_requests.item: How often the bypass is open

where.what: valve position and line temperature
operator logs

data_requests.how: Record bypass position over several shifts.

questions.decision_rule: Prioritize the pump if it runs at a flow 30% or more away from BEP or the bypass is used routinely; otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Five indications: "excessive flow noise, highly throttled flow control valves, heavy use of bypass lines, frequent replacements of bearings and seals, and intermittent pump operation." Prioritize pumps "with flow rates of 30% or more from the BEP flow rates, or with system imbalances greater than 20%." No % saving stated.

questions.limits: A drawn bypass may be normally closed; the drawing cannot show how it is used.

questions.question: Does this pump recirculate flow continuously through a minimum-flow line?
evidence_fields: restriction orifice, MIN FLOW or automatic recirculation valve on a line from discharge back to suction or tank

where.what: clamp-on ultrasonic flow meter on the recirculation line

data_requests.how: Measure both flows at normal operation.

where.what: operator logs

data_requests.how: Count hours with recirculation flow.

questions.decision_rule: Worth action when recirculation flows continuously at normal throughput (an orifice that is always open, or a valve that never closes); an automatic valve that only opens at low forward flow is doing its job.

typical_benefit.wording: "the energy needed to push fluid through bypass lines is wasted." No % stated.

questions.limits: Minimum flow protects the pump; never remove it without the pump vendor's minimum continuous flow.

questions.question: Is this motor oversized for its load?
evidence_fields: motor rating field on the drawing (value or blank)

where.what: motor
motor record card

data_requests.how: Copy rated power, full-load amps and efficiency.

data_requests.item: Measured input power or current at normal load

where.what: a clamp-on power meter (or ammeter plus voltage) at the motor starter

data_requests.how: Measure kW (or amps and volts) over a typical period.

questions.decision_rule: Load factor = measured input power divided by (rated output divided by rated efficiency). A motor running well below about 40% of full load is worth a resize question; one oversized slightly is fine.

typical_benefit.wording: "At loads below 40% of full load, motor efficiency begins to decline dramatically." "Slightly oversizing a motor (up to 25%) can actually increase efficiency." No % saving stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.41xx (category only) (IAC/ITAC browse page: motors: 18,002 recommendations, 2.5 yr average payback, 52.3% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: Fires only where the drawing carries a motor rating field (filled or blank); a drawing without one gives no trigger. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is fan airflow controlled by a damper or inlet vanes instead of speed?

applies_when.absent_note: no speed control on or next to the fan

where.what: damper linkage position

data_requests.how: Note typical and minimum opening and hours.

where.what: fan curve
motor
clamp-on power meter

data_requests.how: Plot the operating point on the fan curve.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a drive quote when the damper normally runs partly closed for long hours; fan power falls with the cube of speed.

typical_benefit.wording: Dampers "remain closed so often that they can be found rusted or locked in a restrictive position... the system continually operates against an unnecessary load." Fan "power is related to the cube of fan speed." No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4146 (by description)

questions.question: Is this compressor spilling flow back (recycle or blow-off) more than surge protection needs?
evidence_fields: recycle / spill-back / blow-off valve on it
its controller and power measurement if drawn

data_requests.item: Recycle (or blow-off) valve opening over normal operation

where.what: anti-surge or recycle controller output

data_requests.how: Take a month or more of valve position; note the hours it is open at normal throughput.

where.what: compressor map with the surge line
the anti-surge controller's surge-line settings

data_requests.how: Compare the normal operating point with the surge line plus the controller's margin.

where.what: power meter at the drive

data_requests.how: Record power with the valve at its normal opening.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when the recycle or blow-off valve is open at normal throughput, or the controller margin is wider than the vendor map needs. If it only opens during upsets or turndown, close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Blow-off "is a waste of energy and should be used only where necessary to avoid surge." Inlet throttling: "Capacity can typically be reduced from 100 percent capacity to about 70-80 percent with reasonable energy reduction." No % saving stated.

questions.limits: Surge protection is a machine-protection function: any change goes through the compressor vendor and a change review.

questions.question: Does a steam pressure-reducing valve between headers pass enough steam to drive a backpressure turbogenerator instead?
evidence_fields: header text on both sides (HP/MP/LP or pressure rating)

data_requests.item: Steam flow through the station over a year

where.what: steam balance

data_requests.how: "Develop steam flow/duration curves for each PRV station".

where.what: gauges either side of the station
header design pressures

data_requests.how: Record both at normal operation.

questions.decision_rule: Consider a backpressure turbogenerator only if the station passes a constant flow of at least 3,000 lb/hr with a pressure drop of at least 100 psi (S6's condition); otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Consider when a PRV has "constant steam flows of at least 3,000 pounds per hour (lb/hr), and when the steam pressure drop is at least 100 psi." Installation costs "typically average 75% of equipment costs".

questions.limits: S6 also quotes cost per kW figures; they are deliberately not repeated here. No IAC code maps to turbines (2.2134 covers PRV-station leaks).

questions.question: Is there a steam trap population large enough to justify a trap survey program?
evidence_fields: count and tags of trap symbols

data_requests.item: Trap inventory and last survey date

where.what: trap list
trap survey history

data_requests.how: Count traps by type and service.

where.what: ultrasonic or thermal survey of each trap

data_requests.how: Classify each trap working / failed open / failed closed.

questions.decision_rule: A survey is likely worthwhile above about 500 traps or when no survey has been done in 3 to 5 years; otherwise fold traps into routine maintenance.

typical_benefit.wording: Unmaintained 3-5 years: "between 15% to 30% of the installed steam traps may have failed." With a program, "less than 5%." LBNL refinery table (as reported in LBNL-56183): trap maintenance 10-15% fuel saved, 0.5 yr payback.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2113 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 445 recommendations, 0.6 yr average payback, 80.1% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is condensate going to drain instead of back to the boiler?
evidence_fields: trap or condensate outlets marked to drain, sewer or grade

data_requests.item: Condensate return percentage and makeup flow

where.what: boiler house makeup and feedwater meters
water and fuel

data_requests.how: Return % = 1 - makeup flow / feedwater flow.

data_requests.item: Contamination risk of each drained stream

where.what: process knowledge of possible leaks into the condensate

data_requests.how: List what could contaminate it.

questions.decision_rule: Worth returning where the drained condensate is clean and the flow is steady; contaminated or tiny streams stay at drain.

typical_benefit.wording: Enthalpy difference "generally over 120 Btu/lb, an amount of energy that is often more than 10% of the energy in the boiler generated steam." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): "Condensate Return Alone 10%", 1.1 yr.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2121 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 354 recommendations, 1.2 yr average payback, 50.9% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is high-pressure condensate flashing to atmosphere when the flash steam could be used?
evidence_fields: flash or vented receiver tag and its vent

data_requests.item: Condensate pressure and flow into the receiver

where.what: pressure gauge and vent plume

data_requests.how: Record pressure and estimate flow.

where.what: steam users list
nearby LP users

data_requests.how: List LP users within reach.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when a steady high-pressure condensate flow vents and a low-pressure user is close by.

typical_benefit.wording: Flash vessels allow "recovery of steam... used in low-pressure steam applications." No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2127 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 31 recommendations, 1.0 yr average payback, 39.3% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is this hot line insulated?

applies_when.absent_note: no insulation code recorded for the line

evidence_fields: line and its stated temperature or steam service

data_requests.item: Insulation condition and length of bare pipe

where.what: infrared camera or surface thermometer along the line
line list insulation code

data_requests.how: Note bare or damaged lengths and their pipe size.

where.what: surface thermometer

data_requests.how: Surfaces over 120 F (49 C) qualify.

questions.decision_rule: Insulate bare lengths over 120 F (49 C) unless they are deliberately bare (for example a line that must cool); closes if the line is already insulated.

typical_benefit.wording: "Insulation can typically reduce energy losses by 90%." "Any surface over 120°F should be insulated." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): insulation 3-13%, 1.1 yr.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2136 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 1,647 recommendations, 2.2 yr average payback, 61.5% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: Many models, and many P&IDs, never record insulation: a finding here means 'not recorded', not 'bare'. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Are large valves and flanges on hot service left bare?
evidence_fields: valve on a line with a stated hot temperature

data_requests.item: Bare valves and flanges by size

where.what: count bare valves and flanges by size; infrared camera

data_requests.how: Count by size and temperature.

questions.decision_rule: Fit removable jackets on bare hot valves and flanges that are not opened often.

typical_benefit.wording: "a 6-inch gate valve may have more than 6 square feet of surface area." The source tabulates heat saved by valve size and temperature. No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2136 (by description)

questions.question: Is boiler blowdown manual, with no automatic control or heat recovery?

applies_when.absent_note: no conductivity element or controller near the boiler

where.what: water treatment log
conductivity of boiler water and feedwater

data_requests.how: Blowdown % = feedwater TDS / boiler TDS.

questions.decision_rule: Automate when blowdown is manual and above what the water treatment needs; add heat recovery on steady continuous blowdown.

typical_benefit.wording: "Blowdown rates typically range from 4% to 8% of boiler feedwater flow rate, but can be as high as 10%." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): blowdown heat recovery 1.3%, 1-2.7 yr.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.124x (IAC/ITAC browse page: 334 recommendations, 1.6 yr average payback, 36.7% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Does this boiler stack have no feedwater economizer?

applies_when.absent_note: no economizer anywhere in the model

evidence_fields: no economizer anywhere on the model

where.what: flue gas thermometer at the stack

data_requests.how: Record at normal firing.

where.what: fuel specification

data_requests.how: Limits how low the flue gas can be cooled.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a quote when stack temperature is high and the fuel allows cooling the flue gas.

typical_benefit.wording: Efficiency "can be increased by 1% for every 40°F reduction in flue gas temperature." An economizer "can often reduce fuel requirements by 5% to 10% and pay for itself in less than 2 years."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.242x (by description) (IAC/ITAC browse page: 635 recommendations, 2.1 yr average payback, 24.3% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Could a condensing economizer serve a cold makeup or process-water heating load?
evidence_fields: cold makeup or process water heating load

where.what: flue gas analysis

data_requests.how: Record at normal firing.

data_requests.item: Size of the low-temperature heat sink

where.what: makeup water flow

data_requests.how: Flow and temperature rise needed.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a quote when a steady cold water load exists near the stack.

typical_benefit.wording: Can "increase overall heat recovery and steam system efficiency by up to 10%." "Simple paybacks... are often less than 2 years."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.242x (by description)

questions.question: Does this boiler or fired heater run without O2 trim?

applies_when.absent_note: no O2 analyzer near the fired equipment

evidence_fields: no O2 analyzer on the flue

where.what: portable combustion analyzer at several firing rates

data_requests.how: Record O2 and CO across the firing range.

questions.decision_rule: Worth trim when excess air is well above what the burner needs across the firing range.

typical_benefit.wording: LBNL boiler table (as reported in LBNL-56183): "1% improvement for each 15% less excess air."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.12xx / 2.121x (category only) (IAC/ITAC browse page: boilers: 4,622 recommendations, 1.3 yr average payback, 56.5% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Does this furnace or fired heater send hot flue gas straight to the stack?

applies_when.absent_note: no recuperator, air preheater, economizer or waste heat recovery anywhere in the model

evidence_fields: no recuperator, air preheater or load preheat

where.what: flue gas thermometer

data_requests.how: Record at normal firing.

where.what: production schedule

data_requests.how: Load preheating suits continuous furnaces.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look for continuous furnaces with hot, clean flue gas.

typical_benefit.wording: "Energy consumption can typically be reduced 5% to 30%." Load preheating is "best suited for continuous rather than batch furnaces."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.241x (IAC/ITAC browse page: 1,936 recommendations, 2.0 yr average payback, 20.0% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is heat rejected to cooling water in one place while steam heats a colder stream in another (a heat-integration question)?
evidence_fields: equipment cooled with cooling water and its temperature tags
equipment heated with steam and its temperature tags

data_requests.item: Temperatures and duties of the cooled and the heated streams

where.what: heat and material balance

data_requests.how: For each stream: supply and target temperature and duty.

data_requests.item: Whether the duties overlap in time

where.what: operating sequence: are both duties needed at the same time?

data_requests.how: Mark each duty continuous, batch or startup-only.

where.what: distance between the two exchangers
cleaning history

data_requests.how: Note pipe run and fouling service.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a pinch or exchanger study only when the hot stream's temperature range sits above the cold stream's with a practical approach, both run at the same time for long hours, and they are close enough to connect. Otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Pinch potential "far exceeds that from well-known conventional techniques such as heat recovery from boiler flue gas, insulation and steam trap management." No % stated in that section.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.243x; 2.244x (IAC/ITAC browse page: 2.243x: 3,673 recommendations, 1.4 yr average payback, 31.2% implemented; 2.244x: 1,466 recommendations, 1.7 yr, 28.6%; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: A screen pairs any cooling-water-cooled item with any steam-heated item; the temperatures decide. On a reactive system any heat-integration change needs a hazard review first. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is the compressed air header pressure higher than the end users need?
evidence_fields: air compressor and its pressure control

data_requests.item: Header pressure profile and the minimum end-use pressure

where.what: pressure at the farthest and most demanding users

data_requests.how: Find the highest pressure any user truly needs.

questions.decision_rule: If the station passes steam only at startup or trips, close this screening investigation; this is not an instruction to operate the station. No source found with a number for desuperheater or bypass stations themselves.

where.what: the site weather station, or the nearest public weather station's hourly record

data_requests.how: Line it up hour by hour with the condensing temperature.

data_requests.item: The lowest head pressure the plant can run at

where.what: the minimum needed for hot gas defrost, liquid injection oil cooling and liquid feed to the farthest evaporator

data_requests.how: This is the floor a floating setpoint may not go below.

data_requests.item: Compressor and condenser fan and pump power

where.what: power logger on the compressor motors and on the condenser fan and spray pump motors

data_requests.how: Floating the head pressure moves load from the compressors to the condenser fans; count both.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when the head pressure sits at a fixed setpoint through cool weather, above both what the condenser could reach and the plant's own minimum. If it already follows the wet-bulb down to that minimum, close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Floating head pressure (S25, p. 62) "allows compressor head pressures to move up or down with variations in ambient wet-bulb temperature, saving energy compared to fixed head pressure operation." Condensing pressure (S25, p. 65): "Lowering the condensing temperature can reduce compressor energy use by around 2% to 3% for every degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) of temperature reduction (SenterNovem 2003)." Condenser fans (S25, p. 65): "On systems where floating head operation is stable, ASDs can lower condenser fan energy consumption by up to 40% compared to operating a fixed-speed condenser fan in on/off fashion (IRC 2004b)."

questions.limits: S25 (p. 62) warns that condenser fan energy rises as head pressure falls and that head pressure must not go below what defrost or liquid injection oil cooling need. Fires only where the equipment's own name, type or service names the refrigerant (ammonia, NH3, R-717, a refrigerant number) or says refrigeration; an air compressor, a process recycle compressor, a process condenser on cooling water or a power-plant air-cooled condenser does not.

applies_when.absent_note: no heat recovery exchanger, recuperator, run-around coil or exhaust recirculation on this unit or on a stream drawn from it

evidence_fields: no heat recovery on the exhaust

where.what: thermometer and a pitot or anemometer traverse in the exhaust duct, at normal production

data_requests.how: Record both at normal production; heat on offer = mass flow x specific heat x (exhaust temperature minus the temperature it could be cooled to).

where.what: humidity or dew point probe in the exhaust; note fat, flour, sugar or product dust
duct and stack cleaning history

data_requests.how: Moist exhaust carries latent heat but condenses; fat and dust foul exchangers unless filtered or washed.

data_requests.item: Fuel or heat input and operating hours

where.what: gas sub-meter readings for this line
production schedule: hours per week the line runs

data_requests.how: A month of input at a known production rate.

data_requests.item: Where the heat could go in the unit itself

where.what: inlet (drying or combustion) air temperature and flow
room next to the unit for ductwork or a run-around coil

data_requests.how: Preheating the unit's own inlet air comes first; H6 asks about users elsewhere.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study when the exhaust leaves hot, the line runs long hours, and the exhaust is clean enough or can be filtered or washed. Close it for short or intermittent runs, or when there is no room for the ductwork.

typical_benefit.wording: Dryers (S26, p. 104): "A simple form of heat recovery in retrofit applications is to utilize the exhaust air of a dryer to preheat the inlet air stream, thereby saving energy." Spray dryers (S25, p. 90): "It is estimated that up to 30% of the heat from the dryer exhaust can be recovered." Fryers (S26, p. 107): "Conditioning of the exhaust gas is required, however, to remove fats and to reduce fouling of the heat exchange system." No source in this set gives a figure for ovens.

questions.limits: S26 (p. 104) notes that recirculating saturated exhaust can raise the inlet humidity and cut drying capacity. A heat recovery item on the unit, or at the other end of a stream drawn from it, quiets the question; recovery drawn elsewhere does not. Ovens and dryers that drive off solvents, or carry combustible dust, need a safety review before any exhaust change.

questions.question: Is the burner air-fuel ratio on this oven, dryer or fryer checked and set, with no flue O2 measurement drawn?

anchor.not_text: AIR COMPRESSOR|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|SERVICE AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|AIR DRYER|DESICCANT|REFRIGERATED (COMPRESSED )?(AIR )?DRYER|STEAM DRYER|GAS DRYER|HAND DRYER|MOISTURE SEPARATOR|COKE OVEN

applies_when.absent_note: no flue O2 analyser or excess air measurement drawn on this unit

evidence_fields: gas- or oil-fired oven, dryer or fryer

data_requests.item: Flue O2 and CO at high and low fire

where.what: portable combustion analyser in the flue or exhaust at high and low fire
the last burner tuning report

data_requests.how: Compare with the burner maker's recommended O2 for this equipment.

data_requests.item: Air-fuel ratio settings and how they are held

where.what: burner management and ratio control settings
burner datasheet: recommended excess air across the turndown range

data_requests.how: Note whether the ratio is fixed linkage, electronic ratio or trimmed.

where.what: gas sub-meter readings for this unit

data_requests.how: A month of fuel use at a known production rate.

where.what: the oven or dryer maker's minimum exhaust and excess air for moisture and solvent removal, and any flammable-vapour (LEL) limit

data_requests.how: This is a floor: the burner may not be tuned below it.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a tune-up when measured flue O2 is above what the burner maker recommends and the process does not need the extra air. On ovens and dryers that drive off water or solvent the dilution and drying air are part of the process: never cut below the maker's or the safety minimum.

typical_benefit.wording: S27 (p. 1): "Periodic checking and resetting of air-fuel ratios for burners is one of the simplest ways to get maximum efficiency out of fuel-fired process heating equipment such as furnaces, ovens, heaters, and boilers." And: "Processes that evaporate moisture or solvents need large amounts of excess air to dilute flammable solvents to noncombustible levels, to ensure adequate drying rates, and to carry vapors out of the oven. Lowering excess air to minimal levels can slow down the process and create an explosion hazard." No typical % stated (the sheet's worked example is one furnace).

questions.limits: Burner adjustment is a combustion-safety change, done by a qualified burner technician under the site's burner management procedures. Indirect (steam or thermal oil) heated units have no burner on them and do not fire this question.

questions.question: Is refrigeration condenser heat rejected while a low-grade heating duty nearby is met with fuel or steam?

AIR COMPRESSOR|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|SERVICE AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|AIR DRYER|DESICCANT|REFRIGERATED (COMPRESSED )?(AIR )?DRYER|RECYCLE|PROCESS GAS|BOOSTER GAS

select.text: HOT WATER|WASH WATER|\bCIP\b|CLEAN.?IN.?PLACE|SPACE HEAT|UNDER.?FLOOR|SUB.?FLOOR|FLOOR HEAT|BOILER FEED|BOILER MAKE-?UP

applies_when.absent_note: no desuperheater or refrigeration heat recovery exchanger anywhere in the model

evidence_fields: a low-grade heating duty (hot water, CIP, wash water, floor or space heating)
no desuperheater or heat recovery drawn

where.what: discharge temperature and head pressure readings in the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.how: Discharge superheat is the hotter, smaller part; condensing heat is larger but only at the condensing temperature.

where.what: compressor run hours from the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.how: Heat rejected is about the compressor power plus the refrigeration load at the same time.

data_requests.item: The low-grade duty: temperature needed, load and hours

where.what: temperatures and loads of the hot water, CIP, wash water, floor heating and space heating users, by hour

data_requests.how: Match by temperature, hours and distance.

where.what: whether a heat recovery exchanger would need a higher condensing pressure than now

data_requests.how: Recovery that raises the head pressure in cool weather costs compressor power (see E27); count it.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study when the refrigeration plant runs at the same times as a duty that needs heat below the discharge or condensing temperature, and recovery does not force the head pressure up. Close it if the duties do not overlap or recovery would need a higher condensing pressure all year.

typical_benefit.wording: S25 (p. 64), refrigeration compressors: "Where economically feasible, rejected heat can be recovered from compressors and used in other facility applications, such as space heating or water heating." No % stated there for refrigeration (the air compressor heat recovery figures quoted under E23 do not apply).

questions.limits: The with-clause finds any low-grade duty in the model, not one next to the plant: distance is for the walkdown. Fires only where the equipment's own name, type or service names the refrigerant (ammonia, NH3, R-717, a refrigerant number) or says refrigeration; an air compressor, a process recycle compressor, a process condenser on cooling water or a power-plant air-cooled condenser does not.

questions.question: Could this oven's, dryer's or fryer's exhaust heat serve a low-grade heating duty elsewhere (hot water, CIP, space heating)?

anchor.not_text: AIR COMPRESSOR|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|SERVICE AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|AIR DRYER|DESICCANT|REFRIGERATED (COMPRESSED )?(AIR )?DRYER|STEAM DRYER|GAS DRYER|HAND DRYER|MOISTURE SEPARATOR|COKE OVEN

select.text: HOT WATER|WASH WATER|\bCIP\b|CLEAN.?IN.?PLACE|SPACE HEAT|UNDER.?FLOOR|SUB.?FLOOR|FLOOR HEAT|BOILER FEED|BOILER MAKE-?UP

applies_when.absent_note: no heat recovery on this unit or on a stream drawn from it

evidence_fields: a low-grade heating duty in the model

where.what: thermometer and a pitot or anemometer traverse in the exhaust duct
production schedule

data_requests.how: At normal production.

data_requests.item: The low-grade duty: temperature needed, load and hours

where.what: hot water, CIP, wash water and space heating loads by hour

data_requests.how: Match by temperature, hours and distance.

where.what: duct or pipe run from the stack to the user; fat, dust or product carry-over in the exhaust

data_requests.how: The closer and cleaner, the better.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study when the exhaust is well above the temperature the duty needs, the two run at the same times, and they are close enough to connect. Otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: S28 (p. 1): "many companies install heat exchangers on the exhaust stacks of furnaces and ovens to produce hot water or to generate hot air for space heating." The same sheet: "The temperature difference between the primary and secondary process should be high enough (at least 200°F), and there should be a sufficient amount of usable waste heat." Fryers (S26, p. 107): "Heat can be recovered indirectly from a fryer's fat-laden exhaust gases via a heat exchange system and used for pre-heating air and water for use in other facility processes." No % stated.

questions.limits: Overlaps E31, which asks about the unit's own inlet air first. The with-clause finds any low-grade duty in the model, not one next to the unit.

questions.question: Is this dryer's or oven's exhaust (and make-up air) rate set by hand rather than by exhaust humidity?

anchor.not_text: AIR COMPRESSOR|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|SERVICE AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|AIR DRYER|DESICCANT|REFRIGERATED (COMPRESSED )?(AIR )?DRYER|STEAM DRYER|GAS DRYER|HAND DRYER|MOISTURE SEPARATOR|COKE OVEN

applies_when.absent_note: no humidity, dew point or moisture measurement drawn on this unit

evidence_fields: no humidity measurement or control on its exhaust

data_requests.item: Exhaust humidity and temperature over a production run

where.what: humidity or dew point logger in the exhaust duct for a full run

data_requests.how: Compare the exhaust humidity with what the product and the process allow.

data_requests.item: Exhaust damper or fan setting and how it is set

where.what: exhaust damper position or fan speed, and whether anything adjusts it
damper position marks

data_requests.how: Note whether it moves with production rate or product.

data_requests.item: Product moisture at the exit and its specification

where.what: quality records: product moisture out of the dryer or oven against specification

data_requests.how: Over-drying shows as moisture well below specification.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when the exhaust leaves well below the humidity the product and the safety limits allow, so heated air is thrown away unsaturated. Close it if the exhaust is already near the allowed humidity or the rate is set by a solvent (LEL) or dust limit.

typical_benefit.wording: S26 (p. 104): "Process controls, such as feedback controllers, feed forward controllers, and model-based predictive controllers, can help to minimize dryer energy consumption by more precisely controlling energy inputs to meet the needs of the product being processed." The sensors it lists include "absorption capacitive sensors (for air humidity)". No % stated.

questions.limits: Exhaust rates on ovens that bake off solvents, or dryers with combustible dust, are set by safety limits: any change goes through the safety review. Fryers are left out: their exhaust is set by the vapour they boil off.

questions.question: Is power to these refrigeration compressors measured, so the plant's kW against load can be tracked?

anchor.not_text: AIR COMPRESSOR|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|SERVICE AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|AIR DRYER|DESICCANT|REFRIGERATED (COMPRESSED )?(AIR )?DRYER|RECYCLE|PROCESS GAS|BOOSTER GAS

applies_when.absent_note: no power, current or energy measurement drawn on these compressors

evidence_fields: refrigeration compressors with no power measurement drawn

where.what: the drive's or motor protection relay's kW reading, or a temporary power logger, per compressor
site interval meter data to apportion

data_requests.how: A representative period at known production.

data_requests.item: Suction and discharge pressures logged at the same times

where.what: suction and discharge pressure per compressor in the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.how: Logged together with power, these show how the plant runs.

where.what: production throughput or freezer and cold store loads by day

data_requests.how: kW per unit of product or per unit of refrigeration.

questions.decision_rule: Meter, or log from the drives, where the refrigeration plant is large enough that kW against load would change decisions; a reading nobody reviews saves nothing.

typical_benefit.wording: S25 (p. 58): "A basic monitoring system should include ongoing measurement and logging of compressor suction and discharge pressures; a drop in suction pressure typically indicates a refrigerant leak, while a rise in discharge pressure can indicate a blocked condenser (EEBPP 2000a)." "In a review of energy efficiency opportunities for refrigeration systems in wineries, the energy savings associated with the installation of monitoring systems were estimated at 3% (Galitsky et al. 2005b)."

questions.limits: The 3% is one review of winery refrigeration, as reported in S25. Fires only where the equipment's own name, type or service names the refrigerant (ammonia, NH3, R-717, a refrigerant number) or says refrigeration; an air compressor, a process recycle compressor, a process condenser on cooling water or a power-plant air-cooled condenser does not.
